title: Ellington's band: improvisation, Vanities and the walking bass
summary: Braud and Russell discuss how little was written out in Ellington's band, Creole Love Call, filming the Vanities and Braud as inventor of walking bass.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Did Ellington write much of that out at all? So when we say like black and tan fantasy, when you make that up?

Well, it comes from improvising. Black and tan fantasy had a score to it, but he had thought that the organization had so many great men in it, they could improvise. And they could put in things that would make Mr. Ellington smile and everybody else, because it was out the ordinary. And the first big band had individuals to get up and play something. What they do in the day was nothing, isn't anything new to Duke Ellington's original orchestra. He had men like Bubba Miley in the small band, and he had men like Tricky Sand. He had men like Bigger in the small band.
One time Barney told me something about how you all took the tune, that was one of Oliver's numbers, I think, in the Camp Meeting Blues. And you were part of that bar, the Creole Love.

Yeah, Creole Love called, and we also, high number we had written by Lorenzo Teal, Mood Enigo. Oh, was that really? Oh, yeah, that was really. But you see, the Ellington is a doctor of music, I'll call him, because he can make a tune a little better and sound a little better than what it is. It'll come from his brain, it still comes from the same thing of improvising. Now, I see in places, I take an eighth note, if it's on the score, and I can make a thirty-second note out of it, but I know where to put it at. Now, if I were playing an arrangement like Rhapsody Blues or a concert number, I could only play it the way the score is, because there wasn't no place to improvise. You know what I mean? Because every note counted in a particular tune of that kind. Now, I had the opportunity of making a picture with the oil cow vanities, the Vanity. And they had a movement in that, for the bass, and the movement of the Hungarian Rhapsody. But only, I rehearsed it down a couple of times, and when I went and rehearsed it a third time, well, we had some dancing girls, the Vanity's chorus. And I see where it was fit that I could swing the second Hungarian Rhapsody movement. And I played it in swing time, and the director thought it was great, and that's what they wanted. But you see, I could tell from the girls dancing, from the taps when they come, when their feet come down, I see where I could build that little girl. See, and that comes from the eyes. The arranger doesn't write that. See what I mean? But after a while, you can sit in the orchestra, and, well, I don't know, I sit just on, besides Elgar's band, that's the only big orchestra. And when I played with Elgar, there wasn't no arrangement, but Duke, the only was the stock arrangement. But Elgin arranges his own music, but then at the same time, he could get a lot of ideas, too, after he would hear a record. And he could get ideas for the bass. And I had men like, I had men like, what's the boy arranged for Tommy Dawson? Cy Alley, huh? To compliment me and told me, Mr. Bro said, I'm very glad to have met you, but we, all of us, learned a lot from your bass and arranged it. Oh. And I think so, because I'm the first man that, that started what we call the walking bass. You see, the walking bass, and I was taught to play bass up and down, you know? Just like a metronome, you know?
